I still remember the first time i could actually see and touch floppy disks. I was, i think 10 or 11.

Back in those days very few people had computers in their houses. I had (and still have) a 8 bit MSX computer and it used only tapes (i didn't have any ROM cartridge)... one of my friends bought a computer, i think it was a Schneider, can't really remember, and it used floppy disks, i think 720K 3.5'' floppy disks, not sure.

They were so blazing fast if compared to my tapes and they looked so cool. It was incredible that so much data could actually fit into something like that. Even the noise it made while reading the disk was cool. I remember that i picked it up from the desk as if it was something both precious and fragile, some kind of technological miracle... today it sounds silly, of course... but today's USB drives just don't give me the same feeling of older floppy disks... while they are certainly a thousand times safer, faster and bigger (in capacity)... it is just not the same, can't even know how to explain it... they just seem less "real" than floppy disks.

Oh yes save it. That beat-up stock may well be battle damage.

Until the very end of the war, these rifles were not captured in large quantities from store rooms or taken from prisoners. They were picked up off the battlefield. Look for embedded metal fragments in the wood.

The rifles that were surrendered at the end of the war had the mum - the flower symbol on top of the receiver - mutilated, either scratched or ground off. A further indication of a battlefield pickup. The mum was the symbol of imperial ownership of the gun.

Do NOT turn any screws - they were staked in place. An unbroken stake is nice to preserve.

Many of these have mismatched bolts, regulations required most to be shipped home with bolts removed, and they were all mixed up when they were handed back out.

These were fine rifles, although they took some shortcuts at the end of the war. Your's looks like an earlier version.

Apply a little oil to the bolt and let it soak in. Do not apply so much that it seeps into and ruins the wood. Give it time, weeks maybe, and maybe it will loosen up enough to open. Just a drop or two in the right spots. Lightly oil the exterior metal to keep the existing rust from growing. I wouldn't do anything else to it.
